uslaw-usc-t1-s106b:
Section 106b of Title 1 of the United States Code covers amendments to the Constitution. It sits in Title 1, on general provisions, in the chapter on acts, resolutions, and the formal steps of enactment. The section states what is to happen when an amendment has been adopted. The trigger is formal notice at the National Archives that an amendment put to the states has been adopted under the terms of the Constitution.

On such notice, the Archivist of the United States must at once have the amendment published. His certificate is to go with the text of the amendment. The certificate states the states that adopted it and that it has become valid for all ends and purposes. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1316b:
Section 1316b of Title 2 extends fair-chance hiring protections to congressional jobs. It sets rights and protections relating to criminal history inquiries. The section borrows its key definitions from a Title 5 provision it names. Agency, criminal history record information, and suspension carry the meanings given there, as modified by this section.

The core restriction follows the same pattern. An employee of an employing office may not ask an applicant for a covered job to disclose criminal history record information. That bar holds where the same request would be barred for an agency employee under the Title 5 rule. A conditional offer rule shapes how the borrowed provision applies. The section sits in Chapter 24 of Title 2, the Congressional Accountability chapter. It falls in the part that extends workplace rights to Congress's own staff.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1816b:
Section 1816b of Title 2 of the United States Code lets the Architect of the Capitol hire services from organizations, not just persons. Personal services contracts are normally made with individuals under a general contracting statute. This section widens the field of who may sign.

Despite any other provision of law, the Architect may contract for personal services with any legal entity. Firms, partnerships, corporations, and associations are all named in the text. Other legal entities are covered by the same phrase. The manner of contracting matches the one used for individuals. That manner is the process set in section 6101 of Title 41, the public contracts title. The single sentence gives the Capitol's keeper access to company expertise on the same terms as individual help.
uslaw-usc-t2-s276b: Section 276b of Title 2 of the United States Code covers travel expenses of the Legislative Counsel of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 9 of that title, on the Office of Legislative Counsel. The rule ties such spending to the rules that bind Senate travel in general. Funds spent by that office for travel are subject to the same rules and limits as Senate travel paid from the contingent fund. Those rules are set by the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.
